source: Raab, Klenk, Medvegy et al. (2026) Intuitive choices in chess option-generation are task and expertise dependent: a conceptual replication
finding: Conceptual replication of a chess take-the-first study in weaker players (mean Elo under 2000). The first generated move was not clearly better than later moves. The take-the-first advantage seems to need high expertise.
numbers: N=92 (original N=34). Players generated M=2.2 options and picked the first generated move as best in 37.3% of cases. Move quality by serial position of generated moves: no significant effect (F(3, 992)=1.73, p=.159).
quote: lower-rated players did not show a clear quality advantage of the first generated option
limits: Quality rated by experts and engine; Elo from online ratings; conceptual not exact replication; first option was descriptively higher but not significant.
agent_relevance: The take-the-first rule is only safe when the generator is expert in the domain. A weak generator needs more candidates and a check. Gate first-option acceptance on a competence signal.

source: Raab et al. (2026), reporting the original Medvegy et al. (2022) chess result
finding: The original chess study, as described in the replication paper: strong players generated few options, often chose the first, and move quality fell from the first to the second to the third generated option. Time pressure hurt weaker players but did not change quality for top masters.
numbers: Original N=34 in three Elo groups (under 2000 M=1659; over 2000 M=2227; grandmasters over 2399 M=2506). Mean options generated M=3.11.
limits: Secondhand account; small selective sample; between-subject design; very high expertise range.
agent_relevance: The evidence for 'the first option is best' comes from the top of the expertise range. Do not generalise to an average generator.

source: Raab et al. (2026) chess replication: task and time-pressure moderators
finding: Intuitive choices were not worse than deliberate choices, but players were especially weak in tactical positions under time pressure. First-move quality differed strongly by position type.
numbers: First-move quality (expert rating) under time pressure: strategic 2.32 vs tactical -1.14 (t=5.66, p<.001, d=0.62 [0.40,0.84]); without time pressure: strategic 2.93 vs tactical -0.60 (p<.001, d=0.52).
limits: Rating scale is relative to engine best move; two to three positions per type.
agent_relevance: Tactical (concrete, calculable) problems are where recognition fails first and a simulation or check is needed. Route exact-answer tasks to checking, not first-option acceptance.

source: Gontar, Porstner, Hoermann, Bengler (2015) Pilots' decision-making under high workload: recognition-primed or not?
finding: In a full-flight simulator with 120 experienced airline pilots, only about a third of main decisions were recognition-primed. Most were analytical comparisons of options.
numbers: 34% RPD vs 66% analytical (n=108 classifiable of 120). The paper compares this with 58% RPD for fireground commanders (citing Klein 1993b).
limits: Coding rule: RPD if no options were compared. Pilots are drilled in an analytical model (FOR-DEC) and their decisions are logged. Simulator, unforeseen events. Not a test of decision quality.
agent_relevance: RPD frequency depends on training doctrine and accountability. Frequency numbers from one domain do not transfer. Our agent should not assume first-option is the usual mode.

source: Gontar et al. (2015), moderators and outcome
finding: Neither flight experience nor remote-association skill predicted who used RPD. RPD and analytical crews were rated equal overall by instructors, and analytical crews were rated better on planning and review behaviours.
numbers: Logistic regression of RPD use on experience and RAT score: model chi-square p=.66 (experience Wald .83, p=.36; RAT Wald .01, p=.92). Overall marker rating RPD vs non-RPD: U=1294, p=.49. Planning: U=1032, p=.02. Review and Modify: U=952, p=.004.
limits: Small effects, instructor ratings are subjective, correlational, crews not individuals.
agent_relevance: RPD use did not buy better rated performance here. Review-and-modify behaviour (a check step) was higher in analytical crews, which fits a check-on-signal design.

source: Klein (2021) The RPD model: criticisms and confusions (Psychology Today)
finding: Klein lists six criticisms and answers them. Key points: the model has two parts (pattern match, then mental simulation); critics say it is unfalsifiable; Klein says random-quality first options would have falsified it; the evidence base is field studies.
numbers: Inexperienced decision makers use the RPD tactic 'less than half the time' (no figure or N given). Cites chess option-generation work (Klein et al. 1995): first option considered was of high quality.
limits: Author defending his own model; blog, no data tables; the claim 'replicated several times' is not backed by citations on the page.
agent_relevance: Author-side evidence only. Treat the falsifiability defence as untested by independent labs.

source: Fire Engineering summary of Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1988) Rapid decision making on the fire ground
finding: Secondary page reports that in 80 percent of incidents commanders handled decision points without considering more than one option.
numbers: 80% of incidents. The original ARI TR 796 was not opened (DTIC returned 403). A 2015 pilot paper cites Klein 1993b as 58% RPD for fireground.
limits: Unit is unclear (incidents vs decision points). Two different headline numbers circulate (80% and 58%). Retrospective interviews, no control group, no outcome measure for option quality.
agent_relevance: Cite the fireground figure as 'about 58 to 80%, unit unclear'. Do not build a threshold on it.

source: Mamede, Splinter, van Gog, Rikers, Schmidt (2012) Salient distracting features and how reflection counteracts diagnostic errors
finding: Residents diagnosing by quick pattern recognition were misled by salient but irrelevant case features. Deliberate reflection cut those errors and raised accuracy. Medical students got no benefit.
numbers: Residents N=34: correct diagnoses 43% (non-analytical) vs 52% (reflective), p=.03; wrong diagnoses triggered by salient irrelevant features 0.85 vs 0.47 per resident, p=.02. Students N=50: 24% vs 25% correct, p=.76.
limits: Secondary analysis of an earlier experiment; salience coded post hoc by five internists; written cases; authors say a causal test is still needed.
agent_relevance: Checking after a recognised first answer pays only when the checker has the knowledge to see the discriminating features. A weak checker adds nothing. Matches G2: revise from real signal.

source: Kuhn, van den Berg, Mamede, Zwaan, Diemers, Bindels, van Gog (2020) Can we teach reflective reasoning in general practice training?
finding: A randomised trial found that practising or studying deliberate reflection did not improve later diagnoses or later reflective reasoning.
numbers: 44 GP residents: control n=14, deliberate reflection n=11, studying models n=19. Same-day accuracy p=.649; delayed (one week) accuracy p=.747; reflective reasoning p=.647.
limits: Tiny cells (11 to 19); one session; read through the abstract page only. A null result may be low power.
agent_relevance: Prompted reflection helps when forced; teaching people to do it unprompted did not work. In an agent, the program must trigger the check; do not trust the model to remember.

source: Mamede et al. (2008) reflection helps on complex cases only (from search summary)
finding: Residents who reflected did not beat pattern-recognition reasoners overall. The benefit showed up only for complex, unusual cases; routine cases showed no difference. Taken from a search snippet only.
numbers: No numbers verified this session.
limits: Not opened. Pointer.
agent_relevance: Supports triggering extra checking on difficulty signals rather than always.

source: Johnson and Raab (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices
finding: Handball players shown video scenes generated options then chose. Option quality tended to fall with each new option, and players switched from a good first choice to a poor final one more often than the reverse. Known only from search summaries.
numbers: 85 German and Brazilian male handball players (secondary report); one thesis cites 60% taking the first option as final (unverified).
limits: Not opened. Video scenes, expert ratings, one sport.
agent_relevance: Core support for 'first option is usually good for experts'. Check the paper before we cite numbers.

source: Raab and Gigerenzer (2015) The power of simplicity: a fast-and-frugal heuristics approach to performance science
finding: Review states the take-the-first rule: generate options in order of validity and stop at the first feasible one. Evidence is from elite team handball and basketball. The tendency to take the first is influenced by situation, emotion and personality.
numbers: Cites Johnson and Raab 2003 (handball), Hepler and Feltz 2011 (basketball), and a rival long-term working memory account (North et al. 2011) which predicts that MORE options means better performance, while take-the-first predicts fewer.
limits: Perspective article by authors of the heuristic; no new data. Transfer claims to nursing, law and navigation rest on single studies.
agent_relevance: A rival theory makes the opposite prediction. The two are separated by whether option count correlates positively or negatively with quality. We can measure that per task.

source: Raab and Gigerenzer (2015), medicine example
finding: Where cues are few and the cost of error is asymmetric, a simple fast-and-frugal tree beat unaided intuition in a chest pain triage example.
numbers: Doctors sent about 90% of chest pain patients to coronary care though only about 25% had a coronary problem (before the tree was used).
limits: Figures quoted from other studies; not independently checked.
agent_relevance: A tiny explicit rule can fix an over-cautious intuition. Rules should live in code, per our guardrails.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: The model plays both agent and world model. It simulates the next state, rewards are self-evaluated, and Monte Carlo tree search explores. This beat chain of thought on planning.
numbers: Blocksworld success with LLaMA-33B: CoT 17%, 2%, 0% on 2, 4, 6-step problems; RAP(10) 100%, 86%, 26%; RAP(20) 100%, 88%, 42%. GPT-4 CoT 50%, 63%, 40%. RAP average 64%, reported as 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT.
limits: Search over many simulated rollouts, not one walk-through. Blocksworld has crisp state. Rewards use the model's own self-evaluation. Compute is many times that of CoT.
agent_relevance: Rollouts of a model-made world help when state is crisp. This is closer to many-path search than to Klein's single walk-through, so it does not test RPD directly.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Letting GPT-4 propose several thoughts, evaluate them and backtrack beat single-chain reasoning on Game of 24.
numbers: Game of 24: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, CoT best of 100 49%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%.
limits: Costs many more calls. The best-of-100 baseline shows part of the gain is just more samples. One game with a checkable answer.
agent_relevance: Even a sampling baseline reaches 49%. Compare against compute-matched sampling (G7) before crediting the simulation.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language agent tree search (LATS)
finding: Tree search with environment feedback plus reflection beat ReAct, Reflexion, ToT and RAP.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1: GPT-4 base 80.1%, LATS (ReAct) 92.7%. HotpotQA exact match (GPT-3.5, acting): ReAct 0.32, Reflexion 0.51, LATS (ReAct) 0.63, LATS (CoT+ReAct) 0.71.
limits: Uses real environment feedback or tests, not pure imagination. Heavy compute.
agent_relevance: Gains come where real feedback exists. Where feedback is imagined only, see the world-simulator numbers below.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Can language models serve as text-based world simulators?
finding: GPT-4 is an unreliable simulator of how actions change a world. Weak spots: changes not caused by the agent, and arithmetic, common sense or science.
numbers: Benchmark of 76,369 transitions. Best accuracy 59.9% on non-trivial state changes. Action-driven changes up to 77.1%, environment-driven up to 49.7%. Humans 80% vs GPT-4 49% on a matched subset. Game progress 92.1% with rules in context, 61.5% without.
limits: Text games, GPT-4 era models. Authors note errors compound: 0.599 to the power 10 is under 1%.
agent_relevance: This is the key limit on 'simulate before you act'. A walk-through is only as good as the model's step accuracy, and errors compound with depth. Cap simulation depth and verify by real execution.

source: Gu et al. (2024) Is your LLM secretly a world model of the internet? (WebDreamer)
finding: Simulating the outcome of each candidate web action in words, then scoring it, beat a reactive agent and came close to real tree search without risky real actions.
numbers: VisualWebArena: 33.3% relative gain over the reactive baseline (real tree search still higher, 26.4% for GPT-4o). Mind2Web-live: +2.9 points, 13.1% relative. Hard multistep tasks still struggle.
limits: Gain is smaller than real search; weak on tasks needing multistep simulation. Reactive baselines only.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to Klein's walk-through: simulate outcomes for a few options and pick the best. It works for one or two steps and fades with depth.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: fast and slow thinking agent
finding: A small fine-tuned fast module acts by default and a large-model planner is called only when the fast module looks stuck. This is an RPD-style split with a trigger.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types: SwiftSage 84.7 average score vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3, with fewer tokens per action.
limits: The fast module is trained on oracle trajectories, so it is not zero-training. Handcrafted switch heuristic. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: switch to slow thinking on a signal, not on a schedule. The fast path needs real experience behind it.

source: Liu et al. (2022) Mind's Eye: grounded language model reasoning through simulation
finding: Running a real physics simulator and feeding its output to the language model fixed basic physics reasoning failures.
numbers: 39 physics tasks: +27.9% absolute zero-shot and +46.0% few-shot on average. GPT-3 175B alone scored 24% zero-shot and 38.2% few-shot. Small models with the simulator matched models 100 times larger.
limits: A real simulator, not the model's imagination. Narrow domain.
agent_relevance: Where an exact simulator exists, call it. Mental simulation by the model is a weaker substitute.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Asking a model to review and fix its own answer, without outside feedback, did not help and often hurt. With the true label as feedback it looked great, which is the trap.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correction after 2 rounds: GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5.
limits: Prompts follow earlier papers; a weak first prompt may inflate others' gains. Reasoning tasks only.
agent_relevance: A model-run 'mental simulation check' of its own answer is intrinsic self-correction. Expect no gain without an external signal. Supports G2 and G3.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the self-verification limitations of LLMs
finding: GPT-4 criticising its own answers made results worse. A sound external verifier gave big gains, and simple re-prompting with a sound verifier kept most of the gain.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Game of 24: standard 5%, LLM critic loop 3%, sound verifier loops 36 to 38%, 25 samples 42%. Graph colouring: 16%, 2%, 34 to 38%.
limits: GPT-4 only; three small domains; one Blocksworld column showed a different pattern, so the collapse is not universal.
agent_relevance: Strong support for code-side checking. Plain resampling (42%) rivals the verifier loop in Game of 24, so always test against equal-compute sampling.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench
finding: Models cannot reliably plan or even reason about the result of their own plan, a prerequisite for mental simulation.
numbers: GPT-4: plan generation 206/600 (34.3%); plan verification 191/600 (31.8%); reasoning about plan execution 141/500 (28.2%); replanning 76.8%.
limits: Blocksworld-style tasks; older models; later models improved. Table columns partly garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: A model's ability to mentally execute a plan is weak. Do not let it self-certify a simulated walk-through.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal reflection on failed trials, stored in memory, improved agents across trials. The gain depends on a trustworthy failure signal.
numbers: HumanEval Python 80% to 91%; ALFWorld ReAct+Reflexion 130 of 134 tasks; MBPP Python 80% to 77% (worse). Test-suite false-positive rate 0.01 on HumanEval Python but 0.16 on MBPP Python.
limits: Uses model-written unit tests as signal; wrong tests give false passes. Gain appears across repeated trials, not in one pass.
agent_relevance: Reflection helps when the failure signal is real. On MBPP the weak test signal made it worse than baseline.

source: Lipshitz, Klein, Orasanu, Salas (2001) Taking stock of naturalistic decision making
finding: Pointer only. Reviews NDM models; not opened because the publisher page was not reachable.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Follow up if a copy can be obtained.

source: Kahneman and Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Search summary: whether an intuition can be trusted depends on a predictable environment and a chance to learn its regularities. Felt confidence is not a reliable sign of accuracy.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not opened; the PDF fetch failed (a university page returned a login page; PubMed needed cookies).
agent_relevance: Gate: accept a first answer only if the task type has stable regularities and feedback. The parallel subfield on conditions for valid intuition covers this.

source: Kaempf, Klein, Thordsen, Wolf (1996) Decision making in complex naval command-and-control environments
finding: Existence confirmed in search (Human Factors 38(2) 206-219, AEGIS cruiser officers). The commonly quoted share of recognition decisions could not be confirmed.
numbers: None verified. The '95%' figure sometimes quoted was not confirmed.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not cite the AEGIS share until the paper is read.

source: Bond and Cooper (2006) systematic review of recognition-primed decision literature in emergency care
finding: Search listing says the review found RPD a good description of acute emergency decisions. No quantitative detail was seen.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the next pass: the nearest thing to a systematic review of RPD.

source: Gap note: independent tests of mental simulation as a decision step
finding: No controlled study of Klein's mental-simulation step as such was found in this pass. Klein's own RPD page lists no sample sizes or replications. Direct tests exist for take-the-first (sport, chess) and for reflection (medicine), not for the walk-through.
numbers: Zero direct experiments found; the page names only the 1985 origin.
limits: Search budget ran out early; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited. This is absence of evidence in a narrow search, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Treat mental simulation in our schema as [S] or [D] until tested on our own tasks.
